subject: Vocabulary
topic: Idioms and Phrases — Meaning and Usage (W11 B1)

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'BEAT AROUND THE BUSH' mean?

options.option_text: To search thoroughly in a jungle
To avoid getting to the main point
To defeat opponents easily
To work very hard in difficult conditions

questions.explanation: B is correct. BEAT AROUND THE BUSH = to avoid coming to the main point; to talk around a subject without addressing it directly. Example: 'Stop beating around the bush and tell me what happened.' Origin: In hunting, beaters would scare game out of bushes by beating around them — not going directly to the bush. Trap: A uses 'bush' and 'jungle' literally; D confuses with a 'hard work' idiom.

options.option_text: To eat something very hard
To take aggressive action
To endure pain or difficulty stoically
To aim precisely at a target

questions.explanation: C is correct. BITE THE BULLET = to endure a painful or difficult situation with courage. Example: 'She bit the bullet and went ahead with the surgery.' Historical origin: soldiers would bite a bullet during surgery before anaesthesia was available to endure the pain. Trap: A takes 'bite' and 'bullet' literally; B confuses with aggressive action; D uses the physical image of 'bullet' and 'aim'.

options.option_text: To make a clumsy mistake
To waste food carelessly
To reveal a secret accidentally
To start a heated argument

questions.explanation: C is correct. SPILL THE BEANS = to reveal a secret, often unintentionally. Example: 'Someone spilled the beans about the surprise party.' Trap: A takes 'spill' literally as dropping something; B uses food context literally; D confuses with 'stir the pot' (start trouble).

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'BURN THE MIDNIGHT OIL' mean?

options.option_text: To waste precious natural resources
To work or study late into the night
To cause a fire by being careless
To finish work very quickly

questions.explanation: B is correct. BURN THE MIDNIGHT OIL = to work or study very late at night. Example: 'She burned the midnight oil to finish her project before the deadline.' Origin: Before electricity, people used oil lamps — burning oil at midnight meant working very late. Trap: A uses 'oil' and 'resources' literally; C takes 'burn' and 'oil' as a fire hazard; D confuses late-night work with speed.

questions.stem: What does 'HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD' mean?

options.option_text: To be very skilled at carpentry
To describe exactly what is causing a situation or problem
To strike something with great force
To start a project at exactly the right moment

questions.explanation: B is correct. HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD = to describe exactly what is causing a situation or to say precisely what is correct. Example: 'You hit the nail on the head when you said the real problem is poor communication.' Trap: A uses 'nail' and 'carpentry' literally; C takes 'hit' and 'force' literally; D confuses 'right moment' timing with precision.

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of 'ONCE IN A BLUE MOON':

options.option_text: Every night when the moon is visible
Only when something extraordinary happens
Very rarely; not very often
Immediately, at this very moment

questions.explanation: C is correct. ONCE IN A BLUE MOON = very rarely; on very infrequent occasions. Example: 'He visits his parents once in a blue moon.' Origin: A 'blue moon' is the rare phenomenon of a second full moon in one calendar month — hence the meaning of rarity. Trap: B (only when something extraordinary happens) captures rarity but adds a condition not implied; D = opposite meaning (immediate).

options.option_text: To start a new enterprise
To fail at a task
To die
To give up an activity

questions.explanation: C is correct. KICK THE BUCKET = to die (informal/humorous). Example: 'He kicked the bucket before seeing his grandchildren grow up.' The exact origin is debated, but it is universally understood as a euphemism for dying. Trap: A uses 'kick' in the sense of beginning or starting; B confuses with 'drop the ball'; D = 'throw in the towel' (give up).

options.option_text: To assist someone physically
To deceive or trick someone
To tease or joke with someone
To persuade someone to do something dangerous

questions.explanation: C is correct. PULL SOMEONE'S LEG = to joke or tease someone in a friendly way; to say something untrue as a joke. Example: 'Don't worry, I'm just pulling your leg — the meeting isn't cancelled.' Trap: B (deceive) is close but incorrect — pulling someone's leg is playful teasing, not serious deception; A takes it physically; D confuses it with a dangerous persuasion idiom.

questions.stem: What does 'A STITCH IN TIME SAVES NINE' convey?

options.option_text: Sewing quickly can prevent nine mistakes
Taking care of a problem early prevents it from worsening
Nine small repairs are better than one large repair
Time management is the key to success

questions.explanation: B is correct. A STITCH IN TIME SAVES NINE = if you fix a small problem immediately, you prevent a bigger problem later (one stitch now saves nine stitches later). It is a proverb emphasising timely action. Example: 'Get the car serviced regularly; a stitch in time saves nine.' Trap: A takes 'stitch', 'time', and 'nine' too literally; C reverses the logic; D oversimplifies to 'time management'.

questions.stem: What does 'BITE OFF MORE THAN YOU CAN CHEW' mean?

options.option_text: To eat too quickly and choke
To be very greedy at a buffet
To take on more responsibility than you can handle
To refuse to accept any help from others

questions.explanation: C is correct. BITE OFF MORE THAN YOU CAN CHEW = to take on a task or responsibility that is too big or too much to handle. Example: 'He bit off more than he could chew by managing three projects simultaneously.' The food metaphor (biting off too much food to chew comfortably) extends to overcommitting. Trap: A and B take the idiom literally (food/eating); D confuses with 'too proud to ask for help'.
